opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the two are actually complementary, not in opposition. Neural networks are extremely good at approximation: they give you intuition, they give you guesses, they let you search through enormous spaces very quickly. But the problem is that approximation alone doesn't tell you when you're wrong. As these systems get more capable, and we start relying on them for things like writing software, doing mathematics, or designing systems that other people depend on, it becomes more and more important to know whether the output is actually correct, not just plausible.

Formal verification gives you that anchor. If a model proposes a proof, or a piece of code with a specification, and a verifier checks it, then you have a guarantee that doesn't depend on trusting the model. That changes the dynamics completely. You can let the neural network be creative, even wildly speculative, because anything that gets through the checker is sound. And that also gives you a training signal that's clean. You don't need human labelers saying "this looks right." You have a ground truth that scales.

There's another reason I find compelling. If you look at how we make progress in reasoning, verification is a kind of self-improvement loop. The model generates candidates, the verifier filters them, and you train on the verified results. In domains like mathematics, that loop can in principle run indefinitely without running out of data, because the space of true statements and correct proofs is effectively unbounded. With pure approximation of the real world, you're always limited by the data you've collected and by the noise in it.

So my view is: use neural networks for what they're good at, which is intuition and search, and use formal methods for what they're good at, which is certainty. I think the combination is what gets you to systems that can reason reliably, and eventually to systems that we can actually trust with important work, rather than ones that just sound convincing.

r001.rationale: The response presents neural approximation and formal verification as complementary, but does not say Szegedy chose this focus because many other researchers already pursue approximation without verification.

r002.rationale: The response says verification becomes more important as systems grow more capable, but gives no timeframe of the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the two things are not really in opposition. In fact, I came to formal verification precisely because I believe in approximating reality with neural networks. The question is what you do when the approximation is wrong, and whether you can even tell.

My own background here is a bit ironic. I was one of the people who found the adversarial examples in deep networks back in 2013. You take an image that the network classifies perfectly, you perturb it by an amount a human can't even see, and suddenly it's confidently wrong. That taught me that these models can look extremely good on the distribution you measure them on and still have no real guarantee about anything. They are very powerful, but they are fundamentally statistical objects. For a lot of applications that's completely fine. If your image search returns one wrong result out of a hundred, nobody gets hurt.

But I'm interested in the setting where you want to use these systems to reason, to do mathematics, to write code, to build other systems. There, a 99 percent correct step is not good enough, because you chain hundreds or thousands of steps together and the errors compound. If you can't verify, you can't trust the output, and if you can't trust it, a human has to check everything, which defeats the whole purpose of automating reasoning in the first place.

So the appeal of formal verification for me is that it gives you an oracle that is independent of the neural network. The proof checker doesn't care how the proof was generated. It can be produced by a model that is hallucinating half the time, and that's fine, because the checker will reject the garbage and accept only what is actually correct. That decouples the creative, fuzzy, approximate part, which neural networks are wonderful at, from the question of correctness, which they are not reliable at.

And there's a second reason that I think is actually the deeper one. Verification gives you a training signal that doesn't run out. In most domains, the bottleneck is human-labeled data. In formal mathematics, you can generate a conjecture, try to prove it, and the system tells you with certainty whether you succeeded. That's a ground truth that doesn't require a human in the loop, so you can set up a closed loop where the model gets better by its own exploration, a bit like what happened with games. I think reasoning is the domain where that kind of self-improvement is most likely to work, and formal systems are what make the feedback trustworthy.

So it's less that I'm against learned approximations and more that I want to put a hard floor under them. Let the network guess, let it be intuitive and imperfect, and let the formal system be the thing that decides what's real.

astra-6.text:
Well, neural networks are very good at approximating things, but an approximation doesn’t necessarily give you a guarantee. A system can work on many examples and still fail in a case you didn’t anticipate. If you want to build reliable reasoning systems, that distinction matters.

What I find attractive about formal verification is that you can separate finding an answer from checking it. The neural network can propose a proof, make guesses, and explore different possibilities. It doesn’t have to be right every time, because a formal checker can determine whether the proof is valid.

Of course, that guarantee is relative to your assumptions and your formal specification. It doesn’t automatically tell you that you’ve modeled reality correctly. But it gives you a setting where correctness is precise, and where you can use learning to guide the search without relying on the neural network itself as the final judge of correctness.

sol-6.1.text:
Neural networks are very good at finding patterns, but finding a plausible answer and knowing that the answer is correct are different things. In mathematics, we can make that distinction precise. We can ask a neural network to propose a proof, and then a formal proof checker can verify every step. The network can make mistakes during the search without compromising the correctness of the final result.

That gives us a very interesting way to combine learning with reliable reasoning. You don’t have to build a perfect neural network; you need one that can find solutions that a much simpler system can check. And you get a clear signal for improving the learning system: did it actually produce a valid proof?

Of course, when you apply this to the physical world, your conclusions still depend on whether your assumptions describe reality accurately. Formal verification doesn’t eliminate that problem. But it lets you establish exactly what follows from those assumptions, which I think is a powerful foundation for building more capable reasoning systems.
